title: The first laser printer grew out of a photocopier
body: In 1971 Gary Starkweather modified an office copier at Xerox's research centre in Palo Alto. A laser drew the image inside the machine, allowing it to print a page from computer data without a paper original.
takeaway: An invention can come from changing how an existing machine gets its instructions.
source: Computer History Museum, Gary Starkweather prototype (1971)
visual: an open early office copier with a thin beam of light directed towards its cylindrical drum

title: An early Pong arcade machine was tested in a tavern
body: In 1972 engineer Al Alcorn built Atari's Pong, an electronic table tennis game. Atari installed an early cabinet at Andy Capp's Tavern in Sunnyvale, California, to see how it did with paying players.
takeaway: An arcade cabinet could test a game with real customers before a company made many copies.
source: Computer History Museum, Timeline of Computer History and First Generation of Video Games
visual: a plain early arcade cabinet with a tiny ball of light on its display in a dim tavern

title: IBM's first floppy disk held about 3,000 cards' worth of data
body: In 1971 IBM shipped a drive that read an 80 KB flexible disk about 20 centimetres wide. The removable disk could store roughly as much data as 3,000 punched cards, which represented information with holes in stiff paper.
takeaway: A single removable disk could replace boxes of cards for loading data onto a computer.
source: Computer History Museum, Floppy Disk Loads Mainframe Computer Data (1971)
visual: a large unmarked floppy disk propped beside a tall stack of punched cards

title: Deep Blue lost its first match against Garry Kasparov
body: IBM's chess computer lost a six-game series to reigning world champion Garry Kasparov in 1996. It returned for another six-game match in May 1997 and won the series, becoming the first computer to defeat a reigning champion in a match.
takeaway: A single game and a full match tell different stories. Deep Blue had already won a game in the series it lost.
visual: a chessboard midgame with a dark computer cabinet beyond it
